walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: sequence and selection

steps.text: This is a different flowchart with the same kind of questions. We try Coins is 18, then Coins is 15.
Begin at Start. Box 2 moves 10 steps. Box 3 says "Go". These boxes run every time.
steps.visual: Steps so far: 10

steps.text: Coins is 18. Is 18 bigger than 15? Yes, so it is True. Box 5 moves 25 more steps.
steps.visual: 10 + 25 = 35 steps

steps.text: Now Coins is 15. Is 15 bigger than 15? No. The same is not bigger, so it is False.
steps.visual: 15 > 15? False

steps.text: The False arrow goes to box 7. It does not move the sprite. The steps stay at 10.
steps.visual: Altogether: 10 steps

steps.text: What does it say last? First box 3 said "Go". Then box 7 says "Wait". The last one is "Wait".
steps.visual: Said: Go, then Wait

steps.text: Now do the same with your flowchart: add the boxes before the decision, then follow one arrow.

steps.label: Do Now: Sub-routines
steps.content:
Do Now: Sub-routines

Think → Pair → ShareWhy put a job in a sub-routine, not draw its boxes again in Main?Show the answer

You draw it once and CALL it as often as you need. To change it, you change one place.

From Lesson 4. Begin at Main's Start.

Total: 3 marks

steps.text: This is a different flowchart with the same three questions. Main is on the left. The sub-routine Skip is on the right.
Begin at Main's Start. Box 1 is CALL Skip. Go to Skip and run all of it: Move 15 steps, then turn.
steps.visual: Steps so far: 15

steps.text: Skip reaches its End. Go back to Main, to the box just after the CALL.
steps.visual: Next in Main: Say "Go"

steps.text: Each CALL runs all of Skip once. Main has 3 CALL boxes, so Skip runs 3 times.
steps.visual: Skip runs 3 times

steps.text: Turns: Skip has one Turn box. It runs 3 times, so the sprite turns 3 times.
steps.visual: Turns: 3

steps.text: Steps: 3 x 15 = 45 from Skip. Main has its own Move 5 steps too. 45 + 5 = 50.
steps.visual: Altogether: 50 steps

steps.text: Now do the same with your flowchart: count the CALLs, then add every Move box.

steps.label: 3.2: Project Plans
steps.content:
Software Development and Physical Computing

3.2: Project Plans

Year 7

  • Today: plan a software project before you build it.
  • The big question: why does a team need a plan?
Think → Pair → ShareWhy might a team of good programmers still not finish a game on time?Show the answer

Good work is not enough. They also need to know what to do, in what order, who does it and by when. Today we learn how.

steps.label: What Is a Software Project?
steps.content:
What Is a Software Project?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy split a big project into small tasks?Show the answer

A small task is easy to start and easy to check. You can see what is done and what is still left.

A project is a big job with a goal and an end date.

  • A software project makes a program, an app or a game.
  • Example: your team makes a Catch game for Sports Day, in one week.
  • It is too big to do in one go. So we split it into tasks.
  • A task is one small job, like "Draw the flowchart".

steps.label: The Stages of a Software Project
steps.content:
The Stages of a Software Project

Think → Pair → SharePredict: why does Design come before Build?Show the answer

You build from the flowchart. A mistake on paper takes a minute to fix. The same mistake in a finished game can take hours.

Most software projects have five stages, in this order.

1. Decide
What must it do? Write a list.
→
2. Design
Draw the flowchart.
→
3. Build
Make it on the computer.
→
4. Test
Try it. Find the mistakes.
→
5. Improve
Fix the mistakes. Test again.
  • Each stage uses what the stage before it made.
  • After Improve, test again.

steps.label: Compare: Design First or Build First?
steps.content:
Compare: Design First or Build First?

Think → Pair → ShareBoth teams make the same Catch game. Which team finishes first? Why?Show the answer

Team Blue. Team Red found the mistake after building, so they built again.

Why? The design shows how the game must work before anyone builds it. A mistake in a flowchart is quick to fix.

Two teams make a Catch game. The fruit must fall faster when the score goes up.

Team Red: build first

  • Day 1 to 3: build the game.
  • Day 4: the fruit never gets faster. Nobody planned it.
  • Day 5 to 6: build it again.

Team Blue: design first

  • Day 1: draw the flowchart. The faster fruit is in it.
  • Day 2 to 3: build the game.
  • Day 4: test. Day 5: improve.

steps.label: Your Turn: Which Stage Comes Next?
steps.content:
Your Turn: Which Stage Comes Next?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does each stage need the one before it?Show the answer

Each stage uses what the stage before it gave. A stage cannot start with nothing.

Type the name of a stage.

Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Activity 1: Put the Tasks in Order
steps.content:
Activity 1: Put the Tasks in Order

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is "Put the tasks in order" the first thing a team does?Show the answer

The order tells everyone what can start now and what has to wait.

Put each project's tasks in order. Then say why. Your progress is saved.

steps.label: What a Project Plan Lists
steps.content:
What a Project Plan Lists

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does every task get a deadline?Show the answer

Everyone knows when their task must be finished. If every task is on time, the whole project is on time.

A project plan organises the tasks of a project. It lists:

PartIt saysExample
Taskswhat to doDraw the flowchart
Orderwhat comes firstTask 2, after task 1
Whowho does each taskNat
Deadlinewhen the task must be finishedTuesday
Needswhat the task needspaper and a pencil

steps.label: Your Turn: Read the Plan
steps.content:
Your Turn: Read the Plan

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a plan put a name next to every task?Show the answer

Everyone knows which jobs are theirs. No job is done twice, and no job is left out.

A plan for the Catch game.

TaskWhoDeadlineNeeds
1. Decide what the game must doPloyMondaypaper
2. Design: draw the flowchartNatTuesdaythe list from task 1
3. Build the gameMintThursdaya computer
4. Test: play it, find mistakesBenFridaythe game
5. Improve: fix the mistakesMintnext Mondaythe test notes
Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Compare: With a Plan, Without a Plan
steps.content:
Compare: With a Plan, Without a Plan

Think → Pair → ShareBoth teams worked hard. Why did only one game work on Sports Day?Show the answer

Team Blue knew who did each task and when. Nothing was done twice, nothing was forgotten, and there was time to test.

Team Red had no plan, so nobody knew which jobs were theirs.

Two teams make a Catch game for Sports Day on Friday.

Team Red: no plan

  • Two people drew the same fruit.
  • Nobody made the score. Each one thought another person would.
  • Friday: no time to test. The game broke.

Team Blue: a project plan

  • Every task has one name.
  • Every task has a deadline.
  • Thursday: test. Friday: the game worked.

steps.label: Why Write a Project Plan?
steps.content:
Why Write a Project Plan?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: which of these reasons stops two people doing the same job? Why?Show the answer

Everyone knows who does what. Each task has one name next to it.

A project plan helps in four ways.

  • You know what to do first, and what has to wait.
  • You finish on time: every task has a deadline.
  • Nothing is forgotten: every task is on the list.
  • In a team, everyone knows who does what.

steps.label: Your Turn: What Is Missing?
steps.content:
Your Turn: What Is Missing?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy check a plan before the project starts?Show the answer

A gap is quick to put right on paper. Found in the middle of the project, the same gap costs days.

A plan for a Space Quiz. It has three gaps.

TaskWhoDeadline
1. Decide: write the questionsPloyMonday
2. Design: draw the flowchart Tuesday
3. Build the quizMintThursday
4. Improve: fix the mistakesBen 
Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Activity 2: What Is Missing from This Plan?
steps.content:
Activity 2: What Is Missing from This Plan?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does one gap in a plan put the whole project at risk?Show the answer

The tasks are joined in order. If one task is late or never done, every task after it waits.

Find the gap in each plan. Then say why it matters. Your progress is saved.

steps.label: Explain: Why a Project Plan Is Useful
steps.content:
Explain: Why a Project Plan Is Useful

Think → Pair → ShareWhat makes an explanation worth 2 marks?Show the answer

Two connected points: what the plan shows, and what that gives the team. Join them with "so".

Your class will make a Catch game for Sports Day, in teams of four.

items.prompt: Explain why a project plan is useful for this project. [2]
items.modelAnswer: It shows who does each task and by when (1 mark), so the team finishes on time and no task is forgotten (1 mark).

steps.label: Practice: Plan the Quiz
steps.content:
Practice: Plan the Quiz

Think → Pair → ShareWhy can some tasks not start until another task is finished?Show the answer

They use what an earlier task gave. A task cannot use something that does not exist yet.

A team makes a quiz for Year 6. The tasks are mixed up.

 TaskWhoDeadline
AAsk Year 6 to try the quizNatFriday
BMake the quiz on the computerMintThursday
CWrite the questions it must askPloyMonday
DDraw the flowchart for one questionPloyTuesday
Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Plenary: Project Plans
steps.content:
Plenary: Project Plans

Think → Pair → ShareWhy practise with a new project every time?Show the answer

If you can plan any project, you really understand planning.

Stages, plans and why we plan. Your progress is saved.
